name: Breatharianism (inedia)

lead: Breatharianism, or inedia, is the belief that a person can live without food, sustained by air, sunlight or spiritual energy. In appearance terms, its appeal is the promise of extreme leanness and a purified, ageless body without eating.

Research comes mainly from reviews of investigated claimants and from medical commentary. A 2020 review of 38 claimants found most cases explained or fraudulent and a few anomalous ones with limited monitoring quality; medical experts consider the practice dangerous.

paras: Practitioners describe gradual reduction of food, spiritual practice and sometimes sun-gazing, with workshops run by teachers. Because of the danger this wiki does not describe procedures.

Going without food and water leads to starvation and dehydration. Deaths have been linked to attempts, including a 1999 case in Scotland and a 2012 case in Switzerland, and the British Dietetic Association calls the diet dangerous.

angle.text: Followers claim that stopping eating yields a lighter, purified body. Medical sources describe the physical outcome as starvation, and no verified route to better appearance is documented.

lead: Breatharianism, also called inedia, is the claim that a person can live without food and sometimes without fluid, sustained by air, sunlight or spiritual energy. Medical experts regard it as pseudoscience, and several followers have died of starvation or dehydration.[1]

In looksmaxxing-adjacent fringe diet culture it is mentioned as the logical extreme of fasting: followers say a body freed from food becomes purified and lean. Wiley Brooks, who founded the Breatharian Institute of America and appeared on television in 1980, and the Australian author Jasmuheen popularised the idea in the late 20th century.[1]

A 2020 systematic review in Explore found 47 investigations of 38 claimants; results were seemingly anomalous in 11 cases, with the review also cataloguing fraud methods and appraising study quality.[2]
infobox: Wiley Brooks, Jasmuheen, Prahlad Jani, Hira Ratan Manek

paras: Inedia (from Latin for fasting) names the claimed ability to live without food. Variants include living on light or on sun-gazing and, in some versions, on water alone.[1]

A 1670 Rosicrucian text credited the practice to Paracelsus, and Hindu texts describe hermits who seemed to live on air. Paramahansa Yogananda's 1946 Autobiography of a Yogi cites two alleged cases.[1]

Wiley Brooks (1936-2016) gained attention on the 1980 television show That's Incredible!, and was seen eating junk food in 1983; he later charged large fees for workshops. Jasmuheen attempted a week-long fast on Australia's 60 Minutes in 1999 but stopped after four days because of dehydration and a rising pulse. She received a Bent Spoon Award and an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000.[1]
Hira Ratan Manek (1937-2022) claimed from 1995 to live on water and sun-gazing; Prahlad Jani was observed at a hospital in Ahmedabad in 2003 and 2010, and critics noted gaps in monitoring.[1]
The body draws on glycogen, fat and muscle when not fed, and extended fasting without fluid leads to dehydration and death. The British Dietetic Association calls the diet dangerous.[1]

Deaths linked to attempts include Verity Linn in Scotland in 1999 and a Swiss woman in 2012; five deaths were linked to Jasmuheen's publications by 2017, three of which she denied responsibility for.[1]
The 2020 review developed criteria for distinguishing normal from anomalous fasting and assessed monitoring quality, and also extracted deception methods seen in fraud cases.[2]
A 2023 survey of 378 people compared emotion regulation among diet 'food tribes', including breatharians, vegans and raw-food eaters.[3]
On T Nation forums, breatharianism appears mostly as a joke or cautionary example, for instance a user noting that it does not seem to work well for those actually deprived of food.[4]
No clinical trials of breatharianism exist. The 2020 review assessed 47 investigations of claimants.[2]

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing and fitness forums, breatharianism is cited mainly as an extreme-fasting curiosity.[4]
